issues.issue: The Representative is named "Kamceo Industrial Products, Inc." while the rest of the instrument and Addendum A call the same party "Kamco Industrial"; the misspelling leaves the identity of the contracting entity open on the face of the document. A court could be asked whether the named entity exists and who is bound as "the Representative."

The authorized line is "items of power transmission equipment sold under the Lovejoy, Inc. name" as specified in "current and subsequent catalogs, bulletins, and other authorized publications," so the product scope is defined by documents the Company alone issues and can change. Both "power transmission equipment" and the catch-all "other authorized publications" leave the boundary of the authorized products indeterminate.

"Directly competitive" is not defined and there is no benchmark (product function, customer, catalog listing) for deciding when a line the Representative carries competes with a Lovejoy product. Because the authorized products in section 1 expand with "subsequent catalogs," the reach of the restraint moves with the Company's publications.

The Company's unlimited discretion to "establish, change, alter or amend prices and other terms and conditions of sale" cannot easily be squared with section 9, which permits commission rates to change only on 30 days' notice by Registered Mail. A court would have to decide whether commission terms are among the "terms and conditions of sale" this provision lets the Company change at will.

The bar on sales to any business "owned, in whole or in part by, or managed by" the Representative has no de minimis threshold, so any fractional ownership interest would trigger it. "Managed by" is likewise undefined as to what degree of control counts.

"All sales policies and operating regulations of the Company" are not identified, attached or limited, so the Representative's obligations are fixed by unilateral documents of unknown content, including the "Windfall Commission Policy" and "Split Commission Policy" referred to elsewhere but not supplied. A court would have to determine what was incorporated and when.

The Territory is only partly stated: "portions of Pennsylvania and New Jersey" is defined solely by "attached territory maps," and no maps accompany the executed agreement. Since commission entitlement under sections 7 and 13 turns on what is "in the territory," the boundary is left indeterminate.

"Exclusive" is not defined — it says nothing about whether the Company or other representatives may sell into the territory — and the four "exceptions" that follow speak only to whether commissions are payable, not to exclusivity. The mismatch between the general grant and the enumerated carve-outs leaves the content of the exclusivity open.

"Export sales" is undefined, so it is unclear whether it excludes only shipments the Company invoices abroad or also in-territory sales to a customer who resells or ships the goods out of the country. The distinction determines commissions on orders otherwise credited under section 7.

"Government contracts" and "accounts classified as Government Accounts (Company Sales Territory 39)" are two different tests, and neither says who classifies an account or whether a sale to a private prime contractor performing a government contract falls inside. The Company's internal territory designation is not otherwise defined in the instrument.

"House Account" is never defined and the Company "reserves the right to redefine these accounts" with no notice requirement or limit, so accounts earning commission can be moved out of commission unilaterally. Addendum A is described only as a "current roster," leaving the operative list a moving target.
